common_name: Suebelle White Sapote (Self-Fruitful Compact White Sapote)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting them in a warm, wind-sheltered spot since young trees are more cold-sensitive than mature specimens.

directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting them in a warm, wind-sheltered spot since young trees are more cold-sensitive than mature specimens. Suebelle stays more compact than seedling white sapote trees, generally topping out around 15 to 20 feet, and it is self-fruitful so a single tree can set a full crop without a pollinator. The smooth green-to-yellow fruit has a custardy, banana-and-pear flavor prized by growers from the warmer parts of the Gulf Coast into Central Florida, and established trees tolerate brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s°F that would seriously injure many other subtropical fruits.

common_name: Meadowlark Blueberry (Ultra-Early Low-Chill Southern Highbush Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container bushes in winter into acidic, well-drained soil enriched with pine bark fines, and mulch to protect the shallow root system.

directions: Plant dormant bare-root or container bushes in winter into acidic, well-drained soil enriched with pine bark fines, and mulch to protect the shallow root system. Meadowlark is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred for only about 200 chill hours, so it reliably leafs, blooms, and ripens even after unusually mild Gulf Coast winters that leave higher-chill cultivars sparse. It is one of the earliest-ripening blueberries available, often ready well ahead of standard rabbiteye types, though it benefits from a second early low-chill cultivar nearby for best pollination. Prune out old canes each winter and fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring to keep plants vigorous.

common_name: Optimus Blueberry (Machine-Harvest Early-Season Southern Highbush Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in winter in well-drained, acidic soil amended with pine bark, spacing plants to allow good air circulation.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in winter in well-drained, acidic soil amended with pine bark, spacing plants to allow good air circulation. Optimus is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred for a very low chilling requirement of roughly 150 to 200 hours, an early bloom period, and good natural leafing, all of which suit the mild, unpredictable winters of the Gulf Coast. The firm, round, medium-sized berries were selected with machine harvesting in mind, and the vigorous, disease-tolerant bushes have shown good field resistance to stem blight and Phytophthora root rot. Home growers get the benefit of a reliable, early-season crop on a tough plant that shrugs off the humid Southern growing season.

common_name: Delite Rabbiteye Blueberry (Extra-Sweet Midseason Southern Blueberry)

planting.note: Set out dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter into acidic, well-drained soil worked with pine bark or peat, and mulch well since rabbiteye blueberries root shallowly.

directions: Set out dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter into acidic, well-drained soil worked with pine bark or peat, and mulch well since rabbiteye blueberries root shallowly. Delite is an older University of Georgia rabbiteye release valued for producing some of the sweetest fruit of any rabbiteye cultivar, with medium to large, light blue berries that ripen midseason. Like other rabbiteyes it needs cross-pollination from a second rabbiteye variety blooming at the same time to set a full crop, and its moderate chill requirement fits well within the zone 7-9 range common along the northern Gulf Coast. The upright, moderately vigorous bushes are long-lived and low-maintenance once established in properly acidified soil.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in winter in acidic, well-drained soil, incorporating pine bark fines to boost organic matter and moisture retention. Released by the University of Florida in 1985, Bonita is one of the earliest-ripening rabbiteye cultivars available, typically flowering and fruiting several weeks ahead of midseason types like Tifblue. It requires a compatible rabbiteye pollinator such as Climax or Beckyblue blooming at the same time to set a good crop, and while modern mid- and late-season rabbiteyes have generally surpassed it in overall yield, Bonita remains a useful choice for gardeners wanting the earliest possible rabbiteye harvest. The vigorous, spreading bush performs well across the humid Gulf South once established in properly acidified soil.

common_name: Joey Avocado (Extreme Cold-Hardy Texas Mexican-Type Avocado)

planting.note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and provide young trees with cold protection for their first few winters.

directions: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and provide young trees with cold protection for their first few winters. Joey was discovered as a chance seedling near Uvalde, Texas, and stands out among avocado varieties for its cold tolerance, with mature trees reported to survive brief drops into the teens Fahrenheit that would kill most avocados. It is a Type B, Mexican-race avocado producing medium, egg-shaped fruit with thin purple-black skin and rich, creamy, nutty-flavored flesh that ripens in late summer through fall. Joey's combination of cold hardiness and dependable production makes it one of the better avocado choices for in-ground planting along the warmer parts of the Gulf Coast and coastal Texas.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Avocado Production in Texas

common_name: Autumn Beauty Jujube (Qiyuexian, Early-Ripening Crisp Fresh-Eating Jujube)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than most fruit trees once established.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than most fruit trees once established. Autumn Beauty, also sold as Qiyuexian, needs only about 400 chill hours and stays compact at 8 to 10 feet tall, with attractive zigzag branching and glossy foliage that turns yellow in fall. The apple-crisp, subtly spicy fruit is prized for fresh eating when harvested at the crunchy green-to-tan stage, ripening earlier than many other Chinese jujube selections. Its low chill requirement and tolerance for hot, humid summers make it a good complement to Gulf Coast-adapted jujube selections like Li and Sherwood.

common_name: LSU Scott's Black Fig (Mississippi-Grown Deep Red-Fleshed Fig)

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting or container tree in spring after frost danger in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; figs tolerate poor soil but reward good drainage and consistent moisture during fruit development.

directions: Plant a rooted cutting or container tree in spring after frost danger in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; figs tolerate poor soil but reward good drainage and consistent moisture during fruit development. Scott's Black is a fig developed by the LSU AgCenter's fig breeding program in the 1950s and, like its siblings LSU Gold and LSU Tiger, was selected specifically for vigor and fruit quality in hot, humid Gulf South conditions. The self-fertile tree produces small to medium figs with deep purple-to-black skin and intensely flavored, strawberry-pink flesh, ripening on a late main crop from September into October. Scott's Black stands out for continuing to produce good-quality fruit into cool, rainy fall weather after many other fig varieties have finished for the season.

common_name: Sweet Frost Mandarin (Cold-Hardy Seedless Changsha-Type Tangerine)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting them in a warm microclimate for extra protection during the coldest nights.

directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting them in a warm microclimate for extra protection during the coldest nights. Sweet Frost is a University of Georgia release bred from Changsha tangerine specifically to make a hardier, more dependable citrus for gardeners as far north as zone 8b, well beyond where most mandarins survive outdoors. The small to medium fruit is easy-peeling and notably sweeter and less seedy than standard Changsha, ripening in fall into early winter. Mature trees have shown better cold tolerance in trials than satsuma, making Sweet Frost a strong option for pushing citrus culture into the cooler fringes of the Gulf Coast.
sources: UGA College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences

common_name: Grand Frost Lemon (Cold-Hardy Zone 8b Culinary Lemon)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, choosing a warm, sheltered spot such as a south-facing wall for extra winter protection.

directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, choosing a warm, sheltered spot such as a south-facing wall for extra winter protection. Grand Frost is a University of Georgia release bred for improved cold tolerance, extending reliable in-ground lemon culture into zone 8b gardens where standard lemon varieties struggle to survive most winters. It bears bright yellow, classically tart, aromatic fruit typical of a good culinary lemon, ripening over an extended season on a vigorous, thorny tree. For Gulf Coast gardeners in the cooler parts of the region, Grand Frost offers a realistic path to growing lemons outdoors with only modest winter protection.
sources: UGA College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; like other kumquat types, Indio Mandarinquat tolerates brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s°F once established.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; like other kumquat types, Indio Mandarinquat tolerates brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s°F once established, better than most true mandarins or oranges. It arose as an open-pollinated seedling beneath a Nagami kumquat tree and was later selected and named at a USDA date and citrus research station in Indio, California, for its unusually large, elongated, bell-shaped fruit. The thin, sweet, edible peel and tart, juicy flesh are eaten together like a kumquat, but the fruit is markedly bigger and juicier than standard Nagami or Meiwa types. Its kumquat parentage gives it cold hardiness comparable to the kumquats already grown successfully along the Gulf Coast, making it a novel option for gardeners who already grow Nagami or Meiwa.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
